hypothesis.title: Flat Minima with Stochastic Weight Averaging Improves Misclassification Detection Beyond Calibration
hypothesis.summary: We hypothesize that combining flat minima optimization with stochastic weight averaging (SWA) improves misclassification detection by enhancing confidence separation between correct and incorrect predictions. Unlike calibration methods that often worsen this separation, our approach uses SAM (Sharpness-Aware Minimization) to find flat minima and SWA to average weights during training, creating a smoother loss landscape. We validate this by measuring confidence separation metrics (e.g., AUC of confidence scores) on in-distribution misclassifications across datasets like CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, comparing against calibrated models and existing flat minima techniques.
hypothesis.gap: Current calibration methods harm confidence separation for misclassification detection, and flat minima techniques are underexplored for this specific task despite their theoretical benefits.
hypothesis.approach: Integrate SAM with SWA during training to enforce flat minima and weight averaging. Use temperature-scaled softmax probabilities as confidence scores. Train ResNet models on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet, then evaluate confidence separation using AUC and FPR@95TPR on held-out misclassified samples.
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include standard training, SAM-only, SWA-only, and calibrated models (e.g., temperature scaling). Metrics: AUC of confidence scores for misclassified vs. correctly classified samples, FPR@95TPR, and comparison of loss landscape sharpness via Hessian eigenvalue analysis.

refined.summary: We hypothesize that combining Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) with Stochastic Weight Averaging (SWA) improves misclassification detection by enhancing confidence separation between correct and incorrect predictions. Unlike calibration methods that often degrade this separation, our approach uses SAM to find flat minima and SWA to average weights during training, creating a smoother loss landscape. We validate this by measuring confidence separation (AUC of temperature-scaled softmax scores) on in-distribution misclassifications across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, comparing against calibrated models and flat minima techniques.
refined.gap: Current calibration methods degrade confidence separation for misclassification detection (ref-002, ref-059), and while flat minima techniques (ref-010, ref-013, ref-022) exist, their specific application to confidence separation remains underexplored. The closest work (ref-002) shows flat minima improve failure prediction but does not combine SAM with SWA for this task.
refined.approach: Integrate SAM with SWA during training: (1) SAM minimizes loss sharpness by perturbing weights with gradient-based noise, (2) SWA averages weights from the final training epochs. Use temperature-scaled softmax probabilities (temperature selected via validation) as confidence scores. Train ResNet-50 models on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet, with identical hyperparameters (learning rate 0.05, batch size 128) for all baselines. The core difference is the addition of SAM+SWA to the optimization process.
refined.evaluation: Baselines: standard training, temperature scaling (calibration), SAM-only, SWA-only. Metrics: (1) AUC of confidence scores distinguishing misclassified vs. correctly classified samples, (2) FPR@95TPR, (3) maximum Hessian eigenvalue (computed via finite differences) to measure loss landscape sharpness. Ablation: SAM-only vs. SWA-only vs. SAM+SWA on CIFAR-10. Test on held-out misclassified samples from validation sets.

hypothesis.title: Flat Minima Optimization for Enhanced Misclassification Detection via Confidence Separation
hypothesis.summary: This work proposes leveraging flat minima optimization techniques, such as Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM), to improve confidence separation between correct and incorrect predictions. By training models in flatter minima, the hypothesis is that the model's confidence scores will better distinguish between in-distribution misclassified samples and correctly classified ones, addressing the gap where calibration methods often degrade this separation. The approach is validated by comparing misclassification detection performance on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet using metrics like FPR@95TPR, showing improved separation without sacrificing accuracy.

hypothesis.approach: Integrate flat minima optimization (e.g., SAM) into training to enforce flatter loss landscapes, which empirically improves confidence separation. Combine with post-hoc confidence scoring to evaluate misclassification detection performance.
hypothesis.evaluation: Compare FPR@95TPR and AUROC for misclassification detection on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet against baselines like temperature scaling and ODIN. Use models trained with SAM vs. standard SGD to isolate the effect of flat minima.

refined.title: Flat Minima Optimization for Enhanced Misclassification Detection
refined.summary: This paper proposes optimizing flat minima in neural networks to improve confidence separation between correct and incorrect in-distribution predictions. By integrating sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) with a modified loss function that penalizes sharp minima for misclassified samples, the method aims to create a more pronounced gap in softmax probabilities. The approach is validated through controlled experiments on ImageNet-1K and CIFAR-100, comparing against softmax baselines and SAM variants using FPR95 and AUROC metrics.
refined.gap: Existing calibration and OOD detection methods (ref-002, ref-059) degrade confidence separation between correct and incorrect in-distribution samples. While recent work (ref-059) connects flat minima to failure prediction, prior flat minima techniques (ref-010, ref-030) focus on generalization without explicitly penalizing sharp minima for misclassified samples.
refined.approach: Use sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) with a modified loss function: L = L_class + λ⋅L_sharpness, where L_sharpness = max_{||ε||≤ρ} [L_class(x + ε) - L_class(x)]. The penalty term L_sharpness is computed only for misclassified samples during training. SAM's ρ is set to 0.05, λ=1.0. Cyclic learning rates (cycle length=100 epochs) and exponential moving average (EMA, decay=0.999) stabilize training. Inputs: training data with labels. Outputs: neural network parameters with flat minima around decision boundaries.
refined.evaluation: Compare against softmax baselines, vanilla SAM (ref-010), and the flat minima method from ref-059 on ImageNet-1K and CIFAR-100. Metrics: FPR95 (target ≤5%) and AUROC (≥95%). Ablation studies isolate SAM's effect on confidence separation (measured by ECE) vs. EMA's contribution. Test on long-tailed CIFAR-100-LT (imbalance factor=100) and ImageNet-C (corruption severity=5) to assess robustness.

hypothesis.title: Masked Image Modeling Pretraining Enhances Out-of-Distribution Detection Without OOD Data
hypothesis.summary: We propose that masked image modeling (MIM) pretraining improves OOD detection by learning intrinsic in-distribution features without requiring OOD samples. Unlike contrastive or supervised methods, MIM forces models to reconstruct missing patches, capturing structural patterns unique to in-distribution data. We evaluate this by training ViT models on ImageNet with MAE pretraining and measuring OOD detection performance on benchmarks like CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 vs. SVHN, comparing against supervised and contrastive baselines.
hypothesis.gap: Existing OOD detection methods rely on parametric assumptions or OOD data during training, while MIM's reconstruction-based pretraining offers a data-efficient, assumption-free alternative.
hypothesis.approach: Pretrain ViT models using MAE on ImageNet, then fine-tune for classification. Use reconstruction error from the pretrained encoder as an OOD score. Test on standard OOD benchmarks (e.g., ImageNet vs. Textures, iNaturalist) using AUROC, FPR95, and compare against post-hoc methods (e.g., ODIN, Mahalanobis).
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include supervised ViT, MoCo-v3, and post-hoc methods. Metrics: AUROC, FPR95, and analysis of feature space compactness (e.g., intra-class variance) for ID vs. OOD samples.

However, ref-036 shows that reconstruction-based methods (like MIM) can outperform outlier exposure methods (which use OOD data) without requiring OOD samples, and ref-045 includes post-hoc methods (e.g., ODIN, Mahalanobis) that do not use OOD data during training. Additionally, ref-060's GradNorm uses only ID data and gradients, contradicting the claim that existing methods rely on OOD data.

The baselines include 'supervised ViT' and 'MoCo-v3' but do not mention whether they are run on the same pretraining/fine-tuning settings as the proposed method, which is critical for isolating the effect of MIM pretraining.

Additionally, quantify feature space compactness via concrete metrics (e.g., average pairwise distances within/across classes) to empirically validate the hypothesis that MIM captures 'intrinsic in-distribution features'.

Reference [ref-060] introduces GradNorm, which also does not use OOD data during training, further undermining the gap claim about MIM being 'assumption-free.'

This would clarify whether MIM's advantage stems from reconstruction specifically or general properties of self-supervised pretraining.

We evaluate this by training ViT models on ImageNet with MAE pretraining and measuring OOD detection performance on benchmarks like ImageNet vs. Textures, iNaturalist, and NINCO, comparing against supervised and contrastive baselines.
refined.gap: Existing OOD detection methods often rely on post-hoc techniques or OOD data during training, while MIM's reconstruction-based pretraining offers an assumption-free alternative. Ref-036 shows reconstruction-based methods can outperform outlier exposure, and ref-045 includes post-hoc methods (e.g., ODIN) that do not use OOD data. However, no work isolates how MIM pretraining alone improves OOD detection without fine-tuning.
refined.approach: Pretrain ViT-B/16 models using MAE on ImageNet-1K, then fine-tune for classification. Use reconstruction error from the pretrained encoder (before fine-tuning) as an OOD score. Test on ImageNet vs. Textures, iNaturalist, and NINCO using AUROC, FPR95. Compare against supervised ViT, MoCo-v3, and post-hoc methods (ODIN, GradNorm) under identical pretraining/fine-tuning settings. Quantify feature space compactness via average pairwise distances within/across classes for ID vs. OOD samples.
refined.evaluation: Baselines: supervised ViT, MoCo-v3, ODIN, GradNorm. Metrics: AUROC, FPR95. Ablations: (1) reconstruction error from pretrained vs. fine-tuned models, (2) comparison against GradNorm (ref-060) to isolate reconstruction vs. gradient-based methods. Datasets: ImageNet-1K (ID), Textures, iNaturalist, NINCO (OOD). Feature compactness measured as mean intra-class distance in the encoder's feature space.

hypothesis.title: Stochastic Weight Averaging with EMA for Robust Failure Prediction in Long-Tailed Classification
hypothesis.summary: This hypothesis explores using Stochastic Weight Averaging with Exponential Moving Average (SWA-EMA) to improve failure prediction in long-tailed datasets. SWA-EMA's ability to find flatter minima and reduce overfitting is expected to enhance confidence calibration for tail classes, addressing the gap where class imbalance exacerbates overconfidence in misclassifications. Experiments on long-tailed variants of CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K will measure failure detection performance using risk-coverage curves.
hypothesis.gap: Class imbalance in long-tailed datasets worsens overconfidence in misclassifications, and existing methods fail to address this systematically (ref-021, ref-048, ref-056).
hypothesis.approach: Apply SWA-EMA during training to improve generalization for tail classes. Combine with a confidence-aware loss (e.g., Correctness Ranking Loss) to explicitly optimize for failure prediction.
hypothesis.evaluation: Evaluate risk-coverage curves and AUROC for failure detection on long-tailed CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K. Compare against baselines like label-aware margin loss and post-hoc calibration.

hypothesis.title: Reconstruction-Based Masked Image Modeling Improves Generalized OOD Detection
hypothesis.summary: This work introduces a reconstruction-based masked image modeling (MIM) framework for generalized OOD detection, where models learn to reconstruct masked patches of in-distribution data. The reconstruction error serves as an OOD score, distinguishing ID/OOD samples without relying on softmax outputs. Experiments on ImageNet and CIFAR benchmarks demonstrate superior detection of both near- and far-OOD samples compared to feature-distance and likelihood-based baselines.
hypothesis.gap: Existing OOD detection methods rely on classification-specific features (e.g., softmax scores) or density estimation, which fail for near-OOD samples and lack generalization to unseen distributions.
hypothesis.approach: Train a MIM model to reconstruct masked image patches, using reconstruction error as an OOD score. Leverage self-supervised pretraining to learn generalizable features invariant to distribution shifts.
hypothesis.evaluation: Compare against Mahalanobis distance, ODIN, and energy-based methods using AUROC/FPR@95TPR on ImageNet (with NINCO, OpenImage-O), CIFAR-10 (with CIFAR-100 as OOD), and medical imaging datasets.

Ref-036 demonstrates reconstruction-based methods (like MOOD) already achieve SOTA without softmax reliance, undermining the novelty of the gap claim.

The baselines (Mahalanobis, ODIN, energy-based) are named but no details are provided on whether they use the same pretrained models or hyperparameters as the proposed method, leaving ambiguity about fair comparison.

Then add ablation studies isolating reconstruction error vs. pretraining effects and specify medical datasets with ID/OOD splits.

refined.title: Reconstruction-Based Masked Image Modeling for Generalized OOD Detection in Medical Imaging
refined.summary: This work introduces a reconstruction-based masked image modeling (MIM) framework for generalized OOD detection, where models learn to reconstruct masked patches of in-distribution medical images. The reconstruction error serves as an OOD score, distinguishing ID/OOD samples without relying on softmax outputs. Experiments on medical imaging datasets (e.g., CheXpert, MIMIC-CXR) demonstrate superior detection of both near- and far-OOD samples compared to feature-distance and likelihood-based baselines.
refined.gap: While reconstruction-based methods like MOOD (ref-036) show promise in near-distribution OOD detection, they lack evaluation on medical imaging domains and do not isolate the contribution of reconstruction error from self-supervised pretraining. Existing methods also fail to generalize to unseen medical distributions due to reliance on classification-specific features or density estimation.
refined.approach: Train a MIM model to reconstruct masked image patches using a ViT architecture with 50% masking ratio. The mean squared error (MSE) between original and reconstructed patches serves as the OOD score. Use self-supervised pretraining on in-distribution medical data to learn generalizable features. The core mechanism differs from MOOD (ref-036) by focusing on medical imaging and isolating reconstruction error via ablation studies.
refined.evaluation: Compare against Mahalanobis distance, ODIN, and energy-based methods using AUROC/FPR@95TPR on CheXpert (ID) vs. MIMIC-CXR (OOD) and vice versa. Include ablation studies isolating reconstruction error (MSE) vs. pretraining effects. Use the same ResNet-50 architecture and hyperparameters for all baselines. Test on both semantic (e.g., different diseases) and covariate (e.g., imaging artifacts) shifts as defined in ref-018.

hypothesis.title: Feature-Space Reconstruction for Out-of-Distribution Detection
hypothesis.summary: This work introduces a reconstruction-based framework for OOD detection by training an auxiliary decoder to reconstruct in-distribution features. The hypothesis is that OOD samples will exhibit higher reconstruction errors in the feature space, enabling detection through a novel energy score combining feature and logit discrepancies. The method is evaluated on ImageNet-scale benchmarks using AUROC and FPR95, showing improvements over distance-based and softmax-based approaches.
hypothesis.gap: Current OOD detection methods rely on parametric assumptions about feature distributions or logit spaces, which fail under complex data shifts. Reconstruction-based approaches are underexplored for OOD detection despite their success in anomaly detection.
hypothesis.approach: Train a lightweight decoder alongside the classifier to reconstruct intermediate features. Define an energy score as the sum of feature reconstruction error and logit-based Mahalanobis distance. Use this score for OOD detection without modifying the classifier's architecture or training objective.
hypothesis.evaluation: Test on ImageNet-1K with iNaturalist and OpenImage-O as OOD datasets. Compare against Mahalanobis distance, ODIN, and ReAct using AUROC (≥92%) and FPR95 (≤10%). Include ablation studies on decoder depth and reconstruction loss types.

assumption.unsupported: The hypothesis claims that 'reconstruction-based approaches are underexplored for OOD detection' (gap), but ref-036 explicitly states that 'simply using reconstruction-based methods could boost the performance of OOD detection significantly' and presents a framework (MOOD) achieving SOTA results. This directly contradicts the 'underexplored' claim. Additionally, the gap's assertion that 'current OOD methods fail under complex data shifts' is unsupported, as ref-046 demonstrates strong performance (90.91% AUROC) on 'difficult OOD benchmarks' using a non-parametric approach (ViM).
assumption.vague: The evaluation section does not specify the exact ImageNet-1K training configuration (e.g., pre-trained model, training epochs, hyperparameters) or the exact implementation of the 'lightweight decoder' (e.g., architecture, loss function). The ablation studies on 'decoder depth' and 'reconstruction loss types' are mentioned but lack concrete details (e.g., which depths/losses were tested, how they were compared). The 'energy score' formula (sum of feature error and logit distance) is not defined with mathematical precision, making replication impossible. The 'logit-based Mahalanobis distance' is cited from ref-023 but not adapted to the new feature-reconstruction context, leaving its integration unclear.
assumption.suggestion: Conduct a direct comparison with ref-036's MOOD framework, which already uses reconstruction for OOD detection, to clarify how the proposed 'energy score' (combining feature and logit terms) differs in both mechanism and performance. Include a controlled ablation where the decoder is removed to isolate the contribution of the 'logit-based Mahalanobis distance' component, ensuring the energy score's added value is empirically validated.

transfer.unsupported: The hypothesis claims that 'reconstruction-based approaches are underexplored for OOD detection' but ref-036 and ref-046 directly address reconstruction-based methods (MOOD) and hybrid feature-logit approaches (ViM) for OOD detection, contradicting this gap claim. Additionally, the hypothesis states that 'current OOD detection methods rely on parametric assumptions' but ref-036's MOOD and ref-046's ViM use non-parametric reconstruction and hybrid scoring, countering this generalization.
transfer.vague: The evaluation lacks specification of (a) the exact ImageNet-scale benchmark splits (e.g., which subsets of iNaturalist/OpenImage-O), (b) the baseline implementation details (e.g., whether ODIN/Mahalanobis are applied to the same feature layer as the decoder), (c) the definition of 'lightweight decoder' (e.g., architecture, parameter count), and (d) the ablation protocol (e.g., how decoder depth is varied, which loss types are tested). The central claim that 'feature reconstruction errors distinguish OOD samples' is not isolated in ablations—no experiment tests reconstruction error alone vs. the combined energy score.
transfer.suggestion: Add an ablation study that decouples feature reconstruction error from the Mahalanobis distance term in the energy score, reporting their individual contributions to AUROC/FPR95. This would test whether reconstruction alone provides signal and validate the necessity of the hybrid approach.

However, ref-036 explicitly demonstrates non-parametric reconstruction-based OOD detection (Masked Image Modeling) that achieves SOTA results without such assumptions. This contradicts the claim that reconstruction-based approaches are 'underexplored' for OOD detection. Additionally, ref-046's ViM method combines feature-space and logit-space signals without parametric assumptions, further undermining the gap claim.
empirical.vague: The evaluation section mentions 'intermediate features' but does not specify which layer(s) are used for reconstruction. The 'lightweight decoder' architecture is not described in terms of layer types/widths. The 'energy score' formula is not provided, making it impossible to reproduce. The ablation studies mention 'decoder depth' but do not define the range of depths tested or how 'reconstruction loss types' were varied. The claim of 'improvements over distance-based and softmax-based approaches' lacks specific baseline comparisons beyond named methods.
empirical.suggestion: Conduct controlled ablations comparing the proposed energy score against its two components (reconstruction error alone vs. Mahalanobis distance alone) to validate the necessity of their combination. This would test whether the claimed synergy between feature reconstruction and logit discrepancies is measurable, rather than assuming it as a design choice.

refined.title: Hybrid Energy Score for Out-of-Distribution Detection
refined.summary: This work introduces a hybrid energy score combining feature reconstruction error and logit-based Mahalanobis distance for OOD detection. The hypothesis is that OOD samples will exhibit higher reconstruction errors in intermediate feature spaces and larger logit discrepancies than in-distribution samples. The method is evaluated on ImageNet-1K with iNaturalist and OpenImage-O as OOD datasets, showing improvements over softmax-based and distance-based baselines.
refined.gap: Current OOD detection methods either rely on parametric assumptions about feature distributions (ref-023) or logit spaces (ref-015), or use non-parametric reconstruction (ref-036) in isolation. However, ref-036 shows reconstruction alone achieves SOTA performance (5.7% AUROC improvement over prior methods), while ref-046 demonstrates hybrid approaches combining feature and logit signals outperform single-modal methods. No prior work combines reconstruction-based feature errors with logit discrepancies in a unified score.
refined.approach: Train a lightweight decoder (3-layer CNN with ReLU) alongside a ResNet-50 classifier to reconstruct intermediate features (layer3 output). Define energy score as E(x) = ||x - D(D(x))||₂ + ||f(x) - μ_c||_Σ_c^{-1}, where D is the decoder, f(x) is the penultimate layer feature, μ_c is the class-conditional feature mean, and Σ_c is the covariance matrix. Use this score for OOD detection without modifying classifier training.
refined.evaluation: Test on ImageNet-1K with iNaturalist and OpenImage-O as OOD datasets. Compare against ODIN (ref-015), Mahalanobis distance (ref-023), ReAct (ref-037), and MOOD (ref-036) using AUROC (≥93%) and FPR95 (≤8%). Include ablations: (1) reconstruction error alone vs. energy score, (2) decoder depth (1-5 layers), (3) loss types (L1 vs. L2 reconstruction).

hypothesis.title: Dynamic Confidence Thresholding via Gradient Norms Improves Failure Prediction Under Covariate Shift
hypothesis.summary: We hypothesize that gradient norms during inference, rather than static softmax scores, adaptively detect failures under covariate shift. By backpropagating a uniform target distribution, we observe that gradient magnitudes differ between in-distribution and shifted samples. We implement a dynamic thresholding mechanism using gradient norms, validated on datasets with synthetic and real-world shifts (e.g., ImageNet-C, CIFAR-10-C), comparing against static confidence-based methods.
hypothesis.gap: Existing failure detection relies on static confidence thresholds, which fail under covariate shift. Gradient-based signals, sensitive to input perturbations, offer a dynamic alternative.
hypothesis.approach: Compute gradient norms of the KL divergence between softmax outputs and a uniform distribution. Train a lightweight threshold predictor using gradient norms and softmax scores. Test on corrupted datasets (ImageNet-C, CIFAR-10-C) and real-world shifts (e.g., domain-adapted ImageNet).
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include softmax baseline, ODIN, and Mahalanobis. Metrics: AUROC, FPR95 for failure detection, and analysis of gradient norm distributions across severity levels of corruption.

transfer.unsupported: The hypothesis claims 'Existing failure detection relies on static confidence thresholds, which fail under covariate shift' but ref-007 and ref-008 show that softmax baselines already perform well under covariate shift (e.g., 'simple softmax response baseline as the overall best performing method'). The gap claim overstates the failure of static methods, as ref-060's GradNorm (a gradient-based method) is already cited as support despite being a static thresholding approach in its original form. The hypothesis also implies gradient norms are novel for failure detection under shift, but ref-060 explicitly addresses this with gradient norms for OOD detection.
transfer.vague: The evaluation lacks a direct comparison with ref-060's GradNorm method, which is cited as support but not explicitly included as a baseline. The 'lightweight threshold predictor' is not described in terms of architecture or training procedure, making replication impossible. The 'real-world shifts' (e.g., domain-adapted ImageNet) are not specified in terms of datasets or corruption types beyond ImageNet-C/CIFAR-10-C. The analysis of gradient norm distributions across corruption severity levels is mentioned but no specific ablation or statistical test is proposed to validate the dynamic thresholding mechanism's effectiveness.

This would clarify whether gradient norms alone (static) or their dynamic thresholding (proposed) provides the improvement, addressing the unsupported gap claim and vague evaluation issue.

empirical.unsupported: The hypothesis claims 'Existing failure detection relies on static confidence thresholds, which fail under covariate shift' but ref-007 and ref-008 show that softmax baselines often outperform advanced methods, including under covariate shift (e.g., ref-007's ImageNet-C experiments). The claim that gradient-based signals are uniquely 'sensitive to input perturbations' is unsupported by ref-060, which only demonstrates gradient norm differences between ID and OOD data, not specifically under covariate shift.

The 'lightweight threshold predictor' architecture is unnamed, and corruption severity analysis lacks a control comparing gradient norms to softmax score sensitivity across severity levels.

However, ref-007 and ref-008 show that softmax baselines already perform well under covariate shift (e.g., ref-007's 'softmax response baseline as the overall best performing method' and ref-008's 'none of the advanced methods can consistently outperform a simple softmax baseline'). This contradicts the claim that static thresholds universally fail. Additionally, the hypothesis states 'gradient-based signals... offer a dynamic alternative' (gap section), but ref-034 shows that no method (including gradient-based) consistently outperforms others across all shift types, undermining the claim of universal superiority.

The 'train a lightweight threshold predictor' (approach section) is undefined—what architecture, training data, or optimization method is used? The 'real-world shifts (e.g., domain-adapted ImageNet)' (approach section) are unnamed; no dataset name or corruption protocol is specified. The 'analysis of gradient norm distributions across severity levels' (evaluation section) is vague—how is severity quantified, and what statistical tests are applied?

Add an ablation isolating gradient norms by comparing (1) gradient-only thresholds, (2) softmax-only thresholds, and (3) their combination, all trained/evaluated identically.

refined.title: Dynamic Thresholding with Gradient Norms and Softmax Scores Improves Failure Prediction Under Covariate Shift
refined.summary: We hypothesize that combining gradient norms and softmax scores with a dynamic thresholding mechanism improves failure prediction under covariate shift. Gradient norms, computed via KL divergence between softmax outputs and a uniform distribution, adapt to input perturbations. We train a lightweight MLP threshold predictor using gradient norms and softmax scores, validated on ImageNet-C and CIFAR-10-C, comparing against static softmax, ODIN, Mahalanobis, and GradNorm baselines.
refined.gap: While ref-007 and ref-008 show softmax baselines perform well under covariate shift, ref-060 demonstrates gradient norms distinguish ID and OOD data. However, no work combines both signals with dynamic thresholding to adapt to shift severity. The gap is the lack of a method that unifies static softmax confidence with dynamic gradient-based signals for failure detection under varying shift levels.
refined.approach: Inputs: softmax scores and gradient norms of KL divergence between softmax and uniform distribution. Output: binary failure prediction. Objective: minimize FPR95 at TPR95. Update rule: train a 2-layer MLP threshold predictor on ID and corrupted data. Component change: dynamic thresholding via MLP. Same: use pre-trained model features. Differs from ref-060: combines softmax and gradient norms in a learned threshold predictor, vs. ref-060's fixed gradient-norm threshold.
refined.evaluation: Setting: ImageNet-C (ref-007) and CIFAR-10-C (ref-008) with 5 severity levels. Baselines: softmax, ODIN (ref-015), Mahalanobis (ref-023), GradNorm (ref-060). Measures: AUROC, FPR95. Ablation: (1) fixed vs. dynamic thresholds on gradient norms, (2) gradient norms alone vs. combined with softmax scores, (3) sensitivity of both signals across severity levels. The ablation isolates the proposed dynamic combination mechanism.

hypothesis.title: Masked Image Modeling Pretraining for Generalized Out-of-Distribution Detection
hypothesis.summary: This work proposes using Masked Image Modeling (MIM) pretraining as a self-supervised strategy to improve generalized OOD detection. MIM's ability to learn structural priors is hypothesized to enhance feature discriminability between in-distribution and OOD samples, addressing the gap where supervised methods struggle with near-distribution shifts. The approach is validated on OpenOOD benchmarks, measuring AUROC for both traditional OOD and near-distribution detection.
hypothesis.gap: Supervised methods fail to capture structural priors for near-distribution OOD detection, while self-supervised approaches like DINOv2 show promise but lack systematic integration (ref-036, ref-040, ref-045).
hypothesis.approach: Pretrain models with MIM (e.g., MAE) before fine-tuning on downstream tasks. Use feature-space distance metrics (e.g., Mahalanobis) for OOD scoring, leveraging the structural priors learned during pretraining.
hypothesis.evaluation: Compare AUROC on OpenOOD benchmarks for traditional OOD (e.g., SVHN vs. CIFAR-10) and near-distribution detection (e.g., ImageNet-v2). Baseline against supervised models and existing self-supervised methods.

assumption.unsupported: The hypothesis claims that 'supervised methods fail to capture structural priors for near-distribution OOD detection' (gap), but ref-036 shows that reconstruction-based methods (like MIM) outperform supervised methods, not that supervised methods inherently fail to capture structural priors. The gap claim overstates the evidence by attributing failure to a specific mechanism (structural prior capture) not directly tested in cited references. Additionally, the claim that 'self-supervised approaches like DINOv2 show promise but lack systematic integration' (gap) is unsupported as ref-040 discusses DINOv3, not DINOv2, and does not address integration for OOD detection.
assumption.vague: The evaluation plan lacks a specific ablation study testing whether the claimed 'structural priors' (approach) are the actual mechanism for improved OOD detection. The description of 'feature-space distance metrics' (approach) is too vague to reproduce (e.g., which Mahalanobis variant, exact feature space used). refined.title: Masked Image Modeling Pre-Training Improves Near-Distribution OOD Detection via Feature Space Geometry
refined.summary: We propose that masked image modeling (MIM) pre-training improves near-distribution OOD detection by learning feature spaces with better separability between in- and out-of-distribution samples. Our method uses MAE pre-training with 60% mask ratio, followed by linear probing for classification. We evaluate OOD detection via AUROC and FPR95 on near-OOD benchmarks (e.g., iNaturalist for ImageNet), comparing against supervised and self-supervised baselines with identical architectures and training conditions.
refined.gap: While ref-036 shows MIM can improve OOD detection, it focuses on far-OOD settings. We address the gap in evaluating MIM for near-distribution shifts, where explicit regularization often fails (ref-063) and feature space geometry is more critical. The closest work, ref-036, does not evaluate on near-OOD benchmarks or analyze feature space properties.
refined.approach: We use MAE pre-training (60% mask ratio, ViT-B/16) followed by linear probing. We compute Mahalanobis distances in the feature space to measure OOD-ness, using the class-conditional covariance matrix from in-distribution data. The core difference from ref-036 is the focus on near-OOD detection and the use of Mahalanobis distance (not reconstruction error) as the OOD score.
refined.evaluation: Baselines include supervised ResNet-50, MoCo v2, and SimCLR trained on ImageNet-1K. We test on ImageNet-1K (ID) vs. iNaturalist-2019 (near-OOD) and CIFAR-10 vs. CIFAR-100. Measures include AUROC, FPR95, and feature space dispersion (trace of covariance matrix). Ablations compare MAE with a non-MIM baseline (SimCLR) under identical conditions.

hypothesis.title: Dynamic Weight Averaging for Calibrated Confidence Estimation
hypothesis.summary: This paper proposes dynamic weight averaging (DWA) as a post-training technique to improve confidence calibration and failure prediction. By selectively averaging weights from training checkpoints based on validation performance, DWA aims to reduce overconfidence in misclassified samples. refined.title: Dynamic Weight Averaging for Calibrated Confidence Estimation
refined.summary: This work proposes dynamic weight averaging (DWA) to improve confidence calibration and failure detection by selectively averaging model checkpoints based on their validation calibration error. DWA assigns higher weights to checkpoints with better confidence separation between correct and incorrect predictions, reducing overconfidence in misclassified samples. The method is evaluated on medical imaging datasets (CheXpert, MIMIC-CXR) using ECE, Brier score, and FPR95, showing improvements over static weight averaging and temperature scaling.
refined.gap: While weight averaging (SWA, EMA) improves generalization, its impact on confidence calibration and failure detection is underexplored. refined.approach: Track ECE and Brier score on a validation set during training. Compute checkpoint importance weights as the inverse of ECE, normalized via softmax. Perform weighted averaging of model parameters, emphasizing checkpoints with better confidence separation. The approach differs from SWA (ref-050) and EMA (ref-022) by explicitly prioritizing checkpoints with lower calibration error, rather than uniform averaging or fixed decay rates.
